name: Wei Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the setting-out lead on a big mixed-use job near the train station, shops on the ground floor and two hundred flats above. Setting out means I mark where every wall, door and socket goes before anybody builds anything, so if I'm wrong by ten millimetres, the whole floor's wrong. I'm on site at seven with the total station, that's the laser surveying tripod, and since spring we've had a little layout robot that drives around the slab printing the wall lines in ink. Afternoons I'm helping the carpentry crews with the tricky bits, stair openings, curved walls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like puzzles, and every floor is a puzzle. I use AI every day, to check drawings against each other, to translate for two lads on my crew whose English is still coming along, and to do the material takeoffs at night. What wears me out is the clash between the drawings and reality, when the architect's model says one thing and the concrete says another. And the commute, forty minutes each way past the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's begin with the first one, AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. On the crew group chat I'd post something like, see, I told you the robot can't make the tea. People already tease me for being the gadget guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit let down, because I'm curious and I like seeing what the next thing can do. But for my family it's fine. Joy, my partner, is a pharmacist, and a quieter future means her job and mine both carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got, keep running the layout robot, keep doing the takeoffs with AI at night. I'd probably do a short course in reading building models better, because that's useful whatever happens. Savings stay as they are, we've got about a year's worth plus a small rental flat Joy inherited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bore you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I started in this trade at seventeen, and the most exciting thing for twenty years was a better nail gun. Then in the last three years it's been drones, laser scanners, the layout robot. I'd miss that feeling of the job moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on your crew who'd be glad to hear AI fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Sam, our oldest chippy, he'd throw a party. He calls the layout robot the Roomba and puts his tea mug on it. I don't blame him, he's got two years to his pension.

S0.say: He'd tell the crew AI is useful but not magic, and joke that the robot still can't make the tea. He's known on site as the gadget guy.
S0.think: Privately he'd be slightly disappointed because he enjoys new technology. But he'd be glad that his and his partner's jobs carry on safely.
S0.do: Keeps using the layout robot and his daily AI tools for checks and takeoffs. Takes a short course on reading building models and leaves his year of savings and the inherited rental flat as they are.
S0.quote: He calls the layout robot the Roomba and puts his tea mug on it.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is the rare tradesman who would find a plateau slightly dull. He uses AI daily, including to help colleagues with weaker English, which shows his inclusive streak. He reads his older colleague's resistance with sympathy rather than scorn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good kind of change if we do it right. At work I'd be showing the younger ones how to use the new kit, and online I'd post videos of the layout robot so people stop being scared of it. I'd also say, loudly, that the savings should go into wages and training, not just into profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do well out of it. People who can talk to both the machines and the crew are going to be worth a lot. My worry is the gap between people like me and people like Big Sam, and who's paying for the ones who fall through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my contracts manager in the first month with a plan to put a second layout robot on the job and train two of the crew on it. I'd do a proper certificate in digital construction at the college, evenings, about eighteen hundred, which I'd pay myself if the company wouldn't. And I'd put some savings into a fund that invests in construction tech, not much, five thousand maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited. With a small voice in the back saying, don't forget about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Big Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I've got his back until his pension. I'd make sure he's doing the work he's best at, the stair strings and the handrails, and not being pushed onto a tablet in his last two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in construction tech while worrying about who falls through the gap. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, and I've thought about it. I'd rather the change happens with people like me in the room than without us. But yes, I'd be making money on the thing that's squeezing people, and I'd want a tax on that, including on me.

S1.say: He'd call it the good kind of change if handled right and post videos to make the robots less scary. He'd also say loudly that savings should go into wages and training rather than profits.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do well, since people who bridge machines and crews will be valuable. His worry is the widening gap between workers like him and older colleagues, and who pays for those who fall through.
S1.do: Proposes a second layout robot and training for two crew members to his manager within a month. Pays about eighteen hundred for an evening certificate in digital construction and puts around five thousand into a construction tech fund.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, with a nagging conscience about others.
S1.quote: I'd be making money on the thing that's squeezing people, and I'd want a tax on that, including on me.
S1.fieldNote: Adaptive and secure, he moves fast and even invests in the change. When the contradiction was named he owned it and turned it into a policy view. His protectiveness of an older colleague is genuine and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, now, with income support for everyone while it shakes out. Online I'd be sharing everything I could about what the robots actually can and can't do, because there'd be a lot of panic and rubbish. At work I'd be honest with the crew, no pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one that gets me. I can adapt, but two years isn't enough for anyone to adapt, not the government, not Joy's pharmacy, not my crew. If AI can do almost any work, it can do setting out, and I'd just be the guy who explains the robot until they don't need me for that either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd try to get a job with one of the companies rolling out the robots, in their site deployment team, because they'd need people who know buildings. I'd hold the savings tight and stop the extra investing. I'd also join a campaign for a public share of the robot profits, something like a dividend everyone gets, and I'd write to my local representative every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own skin so much, but because everybody I know is about to be in the same hole at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ada and Leo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada's eleven, she'd ask if I was getting replaced by the Roomba, because she's heard Big Sam. I'd tell her I might be, and that's all right, because Dad's job is to figure things out. Leo's eight, he'd just want to know if the robot could come to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the robot company. Isn't that helping the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But it's arriving either way in this picture. I'd rather be inside, making sure they don't ship a machine that props a slab badly and gets someone hurt.

S2.say: He'd call for an emergency plan with income support for everyone during the transition. Online he'd share accurate information about what robots can really do, and at work he'd be honest with his crew.
S2.think: Privately this is the scenario that worries him, because two years is too short for anyone to adapt. He knows AGI could do setting out too, leaving him only briefly useful as the person who explains the robot.
S2.do: Applies to a robot company's site deployment team and stops extra investing while holding savings tight. Joins a campaign for a public dividend from robot profits and writes to his local representative monthly.
S2.feel: Anxious, less for himself than because everyone he knows hits the same hole at once.
S2.quote: I'd just be the guy who explains the robot until they don't need me for that either.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptive person on site sees a two-year AGI as beyond anyone's ability to adapt. His anxiety is collective rather than personal, which fits his progressive outlook. He justifies joining a robot firm through safety, showing how practical his idealism is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start on Monday. At the trades college I'd offer to help design a course on running robot crews. Online I'd keep posting, the honest stuff, what works and what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to get two steps ahead. I'd be one of the people setting up the robot sites, and I think I'd enjoy that for a few years. What I can't see is what happens after, when the robots set themselves up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd move into a role managing automated layout and framing on bigger sites, either with my company or a competitor, there are plenty round here. I'd put more into the tech fund, maybe another ten thousand, because if it happens fast that's where the money goes. And I'd get properly involved in the union's technology working group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Interested and uneasy, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm scrambling for one job inside the robot company. With five I'm choosing where to stand, and I can bring a couple of my crew with me. That's the big difference, I'm not just saving myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi and Daniel, the two lads I translate for. They're sharp, they just got stuck on the language. I'd love to see them running a robot crew in five years when everyone wrote them off.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough if work starts immediately and offer to help the trades college design a course on running robot crews. He'd keep posting honest updates online.
S3.think: Privately he's confident he can get two steps ahead and enjoy setting up robot sites for a few years. What he can't see is what comes after, when robots set themselves up.
S3.do: Moves into managing automated layout and framing on larger sites within the first year. Adds about ten thousand to his tech fund and joins the union's technology working group.
S3.feel: Interested and uneasy at the same time.
S3.quote: I'd love to see them running a robot crew in five years when everyone wrote them off.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time turns his scramble into a chance to lift others with him, which clearly motivates him. He still can't picture life after robots self-organise. His mix of investing and union work reflects both his adaptability and his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case of the three AGI pictures, and we'd be idiots to waste it. I'd say we need free retraining, a public dividend and shorter working weeks, all planned now. At work I'd be running sessions at lunch on the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a decade feels manageable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids through school, Joy and I could pay the mortgage off by then if we push. I think I'd enjoy the ride, honestly, and by the end I might be ready to do something completely different, teach or work with the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep in my current job for two or three years and then move into robotic site management. On the side I'd start a small consultancy with a mate, helping smaller builders pick and set up layout and framing robots. We'd overpay the mortgage by three hundred a month and keep a year of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, with an eye on everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been worried about others in every picture. Does that change with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It eases a bit. Ten years is long enough for politics to catch up, if people push. I'd be one of the people pushing, but I'd sleep better than in the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day it actually arrives, in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably take the day off and go fishing with Leo, who'd be eighteen. Then on Monday figure out what's next. I don't think I'd be scared by then, I'd have had ten years to get used to the idea.

S4.say: He'd call ten years the best of the AGI pictures and argue for free retraining, a public dividend and shorter working weeks. At work he'd run lunchtime sessions on new equipment.
S4.think: Privately he sees a decade as manageable, with the mortgage paid off and children through school by fifty-three. He expects to enjoy the ride and maybe move into teaching young people at the end.
S4.do: Stays in his current job for two or three years, then moves into robotic site management. Starts a side consultancy with a friend helping smaller builders adopt robots, overpays the mortgage by three hundred a month and keeps a year of savings.
S4.feel: Calm and curious, still watching out for others.
S4.quote: Probably take the day off and go fishing with Leo, who'd be eighteen.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Wei is at ease, planning a career move and a side business. His concern for others remains but he trusts politics to catch up with enough time and pressure. The image of fishing with his son on the day AGI arrives sums up his settled confidence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd fail, but because nobody gets time, and the people around me get hit before anyone's ready. What would help is a public share of what the robots earn, and training that's free and paid, so people like Kofi and Daniel aren't left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they want to keep. I'd keep the part where you stand on a finished floor with your crew and look at what you did. I don't know if a dividend buys you that.

headlineQuote: I'd keep the part where you stand on a finished floor with your crew and look at what you did.
portrait: Wei Okafor is a 43-year-old setting-out lead on a large mixed-use site, partnered with a pharmacist, with two children aged eleven and eight. He uses AI every day and already works alongside a layout robot, which he finds exciting rather than threatening. He'd find the plateau a little dull, would thrive and invest under steady change, and becomes anxious only under AGI in two years, mostly on behalf of everyone else. With five or ten years he moves into running robot sites, brings colleagues with him and pushes for a public dividend.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because nobody gets time to adapt and the people around him are hit first.
whatWouldHelp: A public share of the money robots earn, plus free, paid training so colleagues like Kofi and Daniel aren't left behind.
